summary: Redwood SE walked Nimbus through OpenTelemetry tracing and token-level metrics design for production LLM inference. Main topics: span model for per-request and per-token tracing, KV cache hit/miss instrumentation, batching visibility, sampling strategy to reduce cardinality, metric labels to keep cardinality manageable, and example Grafana dashboards. Nimbus wants a 48h benchmark on Dedicated capacity and an integration guide. Next steps and owners agreed.
transcript:
Header: 2026-03-30 08:45 PDT | Duration: 65m | Attendees: Samira, Diego (Redwood); Arjun, Lina, Priya, Marcus (Nimbus)

[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Samira from Redwood, I have Diego with me, our SE, we'll do a technical deep dive on observability, OpenTelemetry, and token-level metrics. Can you go around real quick?
[00:12] Arjun: Hey I'm Arjun, infra lead at Nimbus, we run a mixture of k8s clusters and some self-managed VMs, looking to understand how to get visibility into latency and per-token cost.
[00:23] Lina: Lina, ML engineer, I'm focused on model perf and quantization tradeoffs, want to see token-level breakdowns.
[00:30] Priya: Priya from security, quick question: we'll need to confirm KMS integration and audit logs.
[00:36] Diego: Great. Quick agenda: span model, metrics + labels, KV cache instrumentation, batching insights, sampling and cardinality, dashboards and example queries.
[00:48] Samira: Quick note — we'll share the OTLP collector config and a Grafana dashboard JSON after.
[00:55] Marcus: Cool.

[01:05] Diego: Ok jumping in. At a high level we instrument three things: request-level traces (ingress->router->model shard), token-level spans (generation loop per token or per batch of tokens), and async subsystems like KV cache and I/O. The key is linking traces and metrics with a request_id and trace_id so logs can be correlated.
[01:30] Lina: When you say token-level spans, do you create a span per token? That sounds high cardinality.
[01:38] Diego: Good call. We typically do per-token spans in debug/poC modes or sampling; in production we often aggregate tokens into spans per decoding step group — e.g., group of 8 tokens — or emit token counters as metrics with histograms for latency. The spans are optional; metrics are primary for SLIs.
[02:05] Arjun: For Dedicated pools — we want to see tail latency per model version and per customer. What labels do you recommend?
[02:13] Diego: Recommended metric labels: model, model_version, route (api route), customer_id, shard_id, instance_id, batch_size, seq_len_bucket. Avoid high-cardinality labels like full prompt hash or user_id. Use seq_len_bucket like 0-64,65-256,256+.
[02:33] Samira: Also include quantization_profile and runtime_variant where applicable (e.g., int8, int8+kvcache-opt). But keep those bounded labels.
[02:45] Lina: How do you instrument KV cache? We need hit/miss and per-shard memory pressure.
[02:52] Diego: We emit KV cache metrics: kv_cache_hits_total, kv_cache_misses_total, kv_cache_evictions_total, kv_cache_lookup_latency_histogram. Each metric has model/model_version/shard_id and cache_policy labels. For traces, when there's a miss we create a span 'kv_cache.miss' with attributes: lookup_keys_count and fetched_from_storage boolean. Miss spans are sampled at a higher rate to diagnose cold-cache issues.
[03:22] Priya: On the security side, do traces or metrics ever contain PII or prompt content? We can't send prompts to third-party collectors.
[03:30] Diego: Good question. We never include prompt text in traces. Attributes are limited to non-sensitive labels. For customers on Private/VPC we support sending telemetry to their OTLP endpoint — so collector runs in their VPC and we forward metrics/traces there. For hosted mode we can forward to customer's OTLP or push only aggregated telemetry.
[03:55] Arjun: How do we handle Otel sampling and cardinality for token metrics?
[04:01] Diego: Two approaches: metrics-first with low-cardinality labels and optional sampled traces for debug. For metrics, use histograms for per-token latency (token_latency_bucket) and counters for tokens_generated_total. For traces, use probabilistic sampling with adaptive tail-sampling on the collector to keep high-value slow traces. We also use rate-limited debug traces for rare events like kv_cache.eviction or batch_split.
[04:28] Lina: Can you show example prometheus names and a Grafana query?
[04:33] Diego: Sure. Example: histogram name: redwood_token_latency_seconds_bucket{model="rwkv-70b",model_version="v1.2",seq_len_bucket="65-256"} Then SLIs: latency_p95 = histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(redwood_token_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, model, model_version)). For token rate: sum(rate(redwood_tokens_generated_total[1m])) by (model, route).
[05:05] Samira: Note about batching: when requests are batched in the runtime, per-token attribution can be tricky. We emit a batch_size label and also split timing into enqueue_time, batch_build_time, execution_time.
[05:23] Diego: Right — we use spans: request.enqueue, batch.build, batch.exec, decode.step. Each has attributes including batch_id and batch_size. The batch.exec span carries GPU exec duration for that batch; then we normalize per-token by dividing by batch_size for metrics.
[05:45] Arjun: On the deployment side, we want OTLP to go to our collector in the VPC. Is that supported?
[05:51] Samira: Yes — for Private/VPC you can point to your OTLP collector. For Dedicated we can ship to your OTLP or use our collector with egress to your Prometheus, depends on the contract. We'll include config examples.

[06:10] Lina: What about KV cache visibility for on-prem? We often see cold starts after deploys.
[06:16] Diego: For on-prem we recommend startup warmup runs that pre-populate the KV with golden prefixes, and metrics that track kv_cache_fill_rate and miss_ratio over time. We also emit span events when a large eviction happens.
[06:30] Priya: Audit logs — can we have per-request audit trails without prompt data?
[06:36] Samira: Yes, we record request metadata (timestamp, model_version, route, request_id, trace_id, customer_id) and outcome codes. Request bodies (prompts) are omitted unless customer enables prompt logging in a dedicated, air-gapped option and manages encryption keys.

[06:55] Marcus: About dashboards — what out-of-the-box dashboards do you provide?
[07:00] Diego: We ship a Grafana dashboard with: request rate, tokens/sec, token_latency histograms, tail latency panel, KV cache hit/miss, batch_size distribution, GPU utilization, and cost per token estimator. We'll share the JSON.
[07:16] Lina: Can you alias model names consistently? We have internal model tags.
[07:20] Diego: Use model mapping layer at ingestion — sampler or collector transforms: map model hash to canonical name, strip customer-specific suffixes. We'll include a mapping example.

[07:34] Arjun: What about cardinality explosion from labels like instance_id and route?
[07:40] Diego: Keep instance_id optional or downsample it. For route, use high-level route groups instead of full paths, e.g., 'chat', 'qa', 'rerank'. Use seq_len_bucket and quant_profile instead of unique prompt ids. Also use aggregation at collector with relabeling rules.
[07:58] Priya: Any encryption considerations when sending telemetry?
[08:02] Samira: OTLP over TLS, mTLS to your collector is supported. For hosted customers, we can encrypt in transit and at rest; for Private we recommend internal PKI and HSM for KMS. We'll attach our security doc.

[08:20] Lina: Can you walk through a concrete failure scenario — e.g., spike in tail latency after rollout of an int8 quantized model?
[08:27] Diego: Sure. Steps: 1) alert triggers on p99 token latency increase. 2) run traces sampled for p99 traces and inspect batch.exec spans showing longer GPU exec time. 3) check kv_cache_miss rate to see if misses increased (cold cache). 4) check batch_size distribution — maybe autoscaler reduced batch sizes. Combined data points point to either quantization regression or underprovisioned capacity. We keep a 'rollout watch' dashboard that overlays model_version and config changes with SLIs.
[09:05] Arjun: Nice — for the benchmark we want to reproduce our workload with 95th percentile latency <120ms and cost targets.
[09:12] Samira: We'll create a benchmark plan: synthetic traffic with your seq_len distribution, replicate batching, measure token-level latencies, kv cache behavior.

[09:25] Diego: Quick practical notes: exporter settings — keep metrics export interval to 10s for histogram resolution, use OTLP/gRPC for traces, enable tail-sampling rules on collector to capture high-latency traces and kv_cache miss spikes. Limit label cardinality with relabel configs.
[09:52] Priya: Any gotchas for quantization labels?
[09:55] Diego: Include quantization_profile but keep it finite — e.g., none, int8, int8+kv, int4-alpha. Don't create per-weight labels.
[10:05] Samira: Alright let's recap and next steps. Samira: We'll share the OTLP config, Grafana dashboard JSON, and metric name playground. Diego will prepare recommended metrics and relabel rules. Nimbus will provision a Dedicated test cluster and run a 48h benchmark. Security will send KMS and SOC2 requirements.
[10:25] Arjun: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[10:29] Lina: thanks!
[10:32] Samira: We'll follow up with calendar invite for review on 2026-04-06.

End of transcript.
